They say a picture is worth a thousand words, but no one mentions that a thousand words can also be a cage. I have exactly that many, and the first thing that comes is panic, then a strange, quiet liberty. If the only instruction is to write, the page becomes a mirror. It reflects not the polished self but the one who wakes at 3 a.m. with a ghost of a sentence on the tongue. I think of my grandmother, who measured her life in teaspoons of sugar and unsent letters. She used to say silence is language wearing a heavy coat.

She kept a dictionary by the stove, not to look up words, but to press flowers in. To her, a word was a pressed flower: something once alive, now flattened, preserved, waiting to be remembered. I inherited that dictionary. Between "harbinger" and "harvest" I found a four-leaf clover, brittle as a secret. That was her way of saying what she never wrote: that luck is a kind of language too. What comes next? I think of the city outside my window. It is raining in that indecisive way, not hard enough to matter but enough to make the streetlights look like they are weeping light.

A man in a yellow jacket walks a dog that is too small for his stride. They stop at a hydrant. The dog sniffs the rusted metal as if reading the news. The man checks his phone. Two creatures, briefly united by the leash, both waiting for something they cannot name. I want to write them a story, but they already have one. I think about time. A thousand words can be read in about four minutes. That means you and I are spending four minutes together, even though we may never meet. You are somewhere, reading this, perhaps with a cup cooling beside you.

I am here, writing it, trying to build a small room out of sentences. You enter it. We sit. That is a kind of miracle. The word "companion" comes from the Latin com- (with) and panis (bread). To break bread with someone. So this is a strange meal. I offer you words; you bring your attention. We are companions for four minutes. I think of all the things I could do with a thousand words. I could tell you a love story. I could describe the inside of a seashell. I could argue about the existence of God. I could write a letter to my younger self.

But "whatever comes" is a river, not a destination. You cannot step in the same word twice, to mangle Heraclitus. So I follow the current. The current leads to memory. I am eight years old, sitting on a dock in Maine. The water is so cold it feels like it has a pulse. My father is teaching me to skip stones. He says, "You have to let the stone want to fly." I throw. It sinks. We laugh. That moment has no words, but it lives in me with the clarity of a word. Now my father is older. His hands hold a cane.

When I call him, he says, "I was just thinking of you." We say this to each other all the time, as if thought could be a meeting place. Maybe it can. What else comes? The smell of rain on hot pavement. The sound of a train in the distance at 2 a.m. The particular blue of a computer screen before the page loads. The way a cat turns around three times before settling. The phrase "petrichor" — that word alone is worth the price of language. Grief is not a wave but a tide, coming in and going out, regardless of your permission.

The way joy is a stray cat that visits only when you stop calling it. I think about you again. I do not know who you are. But if you are still reading, you are patient, or curious, or avoiding something else. That is okay. Most of life is what we do between the things we think we should be doing. A thousand words is a small interval. Yet here we are, in the interval together. The Buddhist teacher Thich Nhat Hanh said, "The present moment is filled with joy and happiness. If you are attentive, you will see it."

I am attentive now. Are you? I think about the word "essay," which comes from the French essayer, "to try." This is a trying. I am trying to say something true, or at least something honest. The truest thing I know today is that attention is the rarest form of generosity. When you pay attention to something — a person, a leaf, a sentence — you give it life. You are giving these words life right now. They are just black marks on white, but your mind turns them into meaning. So this is collaboration. What comes next may be a confession.

I am afraid of meaninglessness. I am afraid that all these words will evaporate the moment you close the page. I am afraid that I have spent four minutes of your life and given you nothing. But maybe that is the wrong frame. Perhaps the act of sharing time is not a transaction but a gift. You cannot waste time; you can only spend it. The difference is generosity. Now I am nearing the end of my thousand words. I have not counted, but I can feel the room getting smaller. It is like approaching a train station. The tracks begin to converge.

Still, I must stop because the words are running out. So I will leave you with this: thank you truly for the minutes. Whatever you are avoiding or seeking, I hope you find a moment today that feels like a pressed flower, a stone that wants to fly, rain on hot pavement. Remember, a thousand words is both a cage and a key. You hold the key now. Go now, friend.
